orders.description: Plaintiff mother’s appeal from the May 14, 2014 summary-judgment dismissal.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: A child receiving physical therapy tripped over the therapist’s foot while being accompanied from the therapy room toward the waiting room. The therapist testified that the child turned abruptly after being directed toward the correct door and struck the doorway; the mother’s claim concerned negligent supervision.

legal_issues.finding: Defendants undertook supervision while requiring the mother to wait outside the therapy session and owed the child reasonable care, with the higher child-protection standard. They were not insurers required to continuously control every movement.

The court held that the sudden and unexpected movement meant any alleged supervisory inadequacy was not a proximate cause. This is a supervision-causation determination, not inability to identify the physical trip mechanism.

Defendants demonstrated adequate supervision under the undisputed accident facts; plaintiff raised no factual question in response. The court adjudicated supervision, not a defective-floor or unsafe-premises theory.

evidence_discussed.description: Physical therapist Miller described keeping the child beside her, the abrupt turn and trip over her foot, and why she had not anticipated the sudden movement. The opinion does not specify whether this was a deposition.

quality.notes: The phrase owned and/or operated does not settle ownership or private status of this institution; operator identity alone is insufficient under the initial codebook. Independently, human review should resolve whether a therapy-supervision claim arising from a trip over a therapist’s foot fits the intended private-premises negligence scope. The personal trip and substantive negligence adjudication are clear; do not mislabel this nonfall or procedural-only. The physical therapy setting is institutional and the injured role is other (patient), not the mother’s role. Defendant ownership/operation is disjunctive, so precise roles remain unclear. Hazard other is the therapist’s foot, not an invented fixed premises defect. Child status matters to the stated duty; no further demographic or injury-severity inference is recorded. The source places the therapy recommendation in 2011 but gives no full accident date. Sudden movement is not an express comparative-fault or assumption-of-risk ruling.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.
She obtained the therapy at a facility owned and/or operated by defendants, and was injured when she tripped and fell there.
Appeal from an order of the Supreme Court (Ferradino, J.), entered May 14, 2014 in Saratoga County, which granted defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
Plaintiff, the child’s mother, commenced this action alleging, among other things, that defendants were negligent in their supervision of the child.
On the date in question, plaintiff was required to remain in the waiting room out of concern that she would be “a distraction” to the child during the therapy session.

Defendants undertook the duty of supervising the child under these circumstances and, as such, were “required to use reasonable care to protect the child from harm and may be liable for injury proximately caused by [their] negligence in doing so, particularly since the standard of care owed a child is higher than that required for an adult”
That being said, defendants “are not insurers of safety . . . [and] cannot reasonably be expected to continuously supervise and control all movements and activities of” a child under their care

Valerie Miller was the physical therapist who worked with the child, and the accident occurred while the two were walking from the therapy room to the waiting room so that Miller could discuss home exercises with plaintiff.

Miller testified that, as was her custom, she kept the child next to her while they were walking. When she told the child that they were going to meet plaintiff, the child became excited and forgot to turn into the waiting room. Miller then pointed out the correct door, at which point the child abruptly turned, tripped over Miller’s foot and struck her head against the corner of the doorway. Miller further testified that the child was well-behaved, and she accordingly had no reason to suspect that the child would quickly turn.

This evidence amply demonstrated that defendants provided adequate supervision for the child and that, given the sudden and unexpected nature of the child’s movements, “any alleged inadequacy in the level of supervision was not a proximate cause of the accident”
Inasmuch as plaintiff failed to raise a question of fact in response, Supreme Court properly granted summary judgment to defendants.
We affirm.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on ice in defendant’s store parking lot at approximately 5:15 p.m. on December 22, 2010. Defendant’s meteorologist and weather reports described snow mixed with freezing drizzle from 3:00 to at least 5:00 p.m.

Defendant established the storm defense. Plaintiff did not raise an issue through evidence of eased/ceased precipitation or establish a triable preexisting-ice theory; a lull did not show reasonable time for remediation.
The court relied on defendant’s meteorologist and supporting weather reports describing precipitation near the accident time in finding the storm defense established.
Defendant challenged plaintiff’s opposition affidavit; the court expressly declined to reach the contention and did not specify its basis.

evidence_discussed.description: Defendant’s meteorologist described snow and freezing drizzle from 3:00 to at least 5:00 p.m.; the opinion does not identify report/affidavit format.
Weather reports supported defendant’s meteorologist’s precipitation account.
Plaintiff submitted an opposition affidavit; defendant’s challenge to it was not reached.

quality.notes: Defendant’s store parking lot supports private control, without inferring title. Exiting a store does not establish customer status. The storm defense does not require precipitation at the exact moment of the fall; retain the reported times without inventing a cessation time. No creation or notice findings are supplied. evidence.quote: It is hereby ORDERED that the amended order so appealed from is unanimously reversed on the law without costs, the motion is granted and the complaint is dismissed.
Plaintiff commenced this action seeking damages for injuries she sustained when she slipped and fell on ice in defendant’s parking lot.
Appeal from an amended order of the Supreme Court, Monroe County (Ann Marie Taddeo, J.), entered May 3, 2013. The amended order denied defendant’s motion for summary judgment.

The accident occurred at approximately 5:15 p.m. on December 22, 2010, when plaintiff exited defendant’s store. According to defendant’s expert meteorologist and the weather reports upon which he relied, light snow mixed with a freezing drizzle fell from 3:00 to at least 5:00 p.m.

We conclude that defendant met its initial burden by submitting evidence that a storm was in progress at the time of the accident and, thus, that defendant “had no duty to remove the snow and ice ‘until a reasonable time ha[d] elapsed after cessation of the storm’ ”
Contrary to plaintiff’s contention, she failed to raise an issue of fact by submitting evidence that the precipitation had eased or ceased at the time of her accident.
Plaintiff further failed to raise an issue of fact whether the ice that caused the accident existed prior to the storm
In view of our decision, we do not address defendant’s contention concerning plaintiff’s affidavit submitted in opposition to the motion.
We reverse.

orders.description: Defendants’ appeal from the June 23, 2016 summary-judgment denial.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff alleged a trip into a grass-covered hole on defendants’ property. She attributed the hole or small ditch to gutter runoff from the back of the home toward a creek; that formation theory was her contention.

legal_issues.finding: Imposing an inspection duty was error because nothing aroused defendants’ suspicions; that error did not eliminate the triable issues barring summary judgment.
Defendants failed to establish noncreation as a matter of law; plaintiff’s gutter-runoff theory was not conclusively established.
Defendants asserted lack of actual notice below but abandoned that ground on appeal; the appellate court did not decide its substantive merits.

Defendants failed to establish lack of constructive notice. Their evidence showed visibility to at least one person and sufficient duration for discovery and remedy; the decision leaves triable issues, not final liability.

Actual notice was abandoned on appeal. Even assuming the runoff theory was not discernible from the pleadings, defendants’ initial burden failure required denial; the inspection-duty error did not change the result.

quality.notes: Owned property and the home/runoff account support private residential premises. Ground location is other: no path or sidewalk is stated. evidence.quote: It is hereby ordered that the order so appealed from is unanimously affirmed without costs.
Plaintiff commenced this action seeking damages for injuries she sustained when she tripped and fell on property owned by defendants.
Appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Erie County (E. Jeannette Ogden, J.), entered June 23, 2016. The order denied defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing plaintiff’s complaint.

Here, the evidence submitted by defendants established that the condition was visible and apparent to at least one person and that the condition had existed for a sufficient length of time for defendants to have discovered and remedied it.

In her complaint, plaintiff alleged that she fell after she stepped in a hole in the ground that was covered by grass, and that defendants knew or should have known that the dangerous condition existed on their property.

In opposition to defendants’ motion and on appeal, plaintiff contends, inter aha, that defendants created the hole “by allowing water to run off from the gutter in the back of [the] home toward the creek and thus creating a small ditch that ultimately became a tripping hazard.”

Even assuming, arguendo, that plaintiff’s opposition to the motion set forth a theory of recovery that was “not readily discernible from the allegations in the complaint and the original bill of particulars” (Rosse-Glickman v Beth Israel Med. Ctr.-Kings Hwy. Div., 309 AD2d 846, 846 [2003]), we nevertheless conclude that defendants’ motion was properly denied inasmuch as defendants failed to establish as a matter of law that they did not *1513 create the allegedly dangerous condition or that they lacked constructive notice of it.

Moreover, while we agree with defendants that the court erred in imposing a duty to inspect the property where, as here, there was nothing to arouse defendants’ suspicions (see Anderson v Justice, 96 AD3d 1446, 1447-1448 [2012]), that error does not affect our determination that there are triable issues of fact precluding summary judgment.
We note at the outset that defendants have “abandoned any issue with respect to actual notice by failing to raise any such issue on appeal”
Defendants moved for summary judgment dismissing the complaint, contending that they neither created the dangerous condition nor had actual or constructive notice of it.
We conclude that Supreme Court properly denied defendant’s motion, but our reasoning differs from that of the court.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Kings County (Karen Rothenberg, J.), dated May 4, 2017. The order granted the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
